title: Evaluating a Deterministic Validator Plus Single‑Iteration Repair Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configurations
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment (N=300 paired intent→configuration tasks; preregistration id cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1) to test whether a minimal guarded pipeline—single‑shot LLM generation (declared model: gpt-5-mini) followed by a frozen deterministic configuration validator and at most one automated repair iteration—reduces first‑pass misconfiguration versus plain single‑shot generation. Execution completed 600 episodes and used 301 model calls. Observed outcomes: baseline = 299/300 valid (99.667%); guarded = 300/300 valid (100.0%); paired counts n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; absolute paired difference = 0.0033333; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). The single permitted automated repair corrected the sole invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1; Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]). The preregistered planning assumption (planned baseline pass rate = 0.40) was contradicted by the observed near‑ceiling baseline, removing statistical headroom for the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction target. We report preregistered design choices (preregistration SHA-256: 4a00a81629acfd3f1fb5d0a04cea795a52261270e7dc63bf7d3cb63cc11afda0), execution accounting, confirmatory statistics, a concise post‑hoc sensitivity bound tied to the archived contingency counts, and artifact‑grounded recommendations for future NetOps confirmatory evaluations. All run artifacts and analysis outputs are archived in the execution manifest and analysis artifact bundle referenced in the Disclosure Statement.

sections.introduction:
Translating operator intent into device configuration is a foundational NetOps task. Large language models (LLMs) can produce readable configuration artifacts from natural‑language intent, but probabilistic generation risks misordering, omission, or unsafe commands. A common safety pattern is generate→verify→repair: a probabilistic generator produces a candidate, a deterministic validator (or simulator) checks constraints and dependencies, and an automated or human repair loop corrects detected violations. Prior surveys and system papers motivate this pattern, yet few preregistered paired experiments quantify whether a bounded guarded pipeline materially reduces first‑pass misconfiguration rates under controlled sampling.

This work implements a narrowly scoped, preregistered paired experiment to measure the effect of a minimal guarded pipeline: a single shared LLM candidate per task (single‑shot), a frozen deterministic configuration validator that applies rule and dependency checks and canonicalization to normalized ASTs, and at most one automated repair iteration when the validator signals violations. The primary research question is: Can this minimal guarded pipeline reduce first‑pass misconfiguration rate relative to plain single‑shot generation under the preregistered paired design? We preserve all archived artifacts and report exact archived counts and intervals rather than derived approximations.
sections.related_work: Empirical demonstrations show LLMs can synthesize configuration templates and perform intent→configuration translation in controlled settings, but characterize systematic failure modes (hallucination, misordering, overconfidence) that threaten operational safety. Cross‑domain studies (medical QA, code repair) document that retrieval augmentation, deterministic verifiers, and bounded repair loops reduce factual errors and improve grounding; NetOps architectural proposals likewise advocate deterministic validators as floor‑safety nets and bounded generate→verify→repair pipelines for agentic workflows. Our contribution is a preregistered, paired confirmatory test of a minimal guarded pipeline with deterministic seeds, frozen validator logic, a one‑iteration repair budget, and full artifact archival to permit direct verification of reported counts and intervals.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and hypotheses: The study preregistration (cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1) froze design choices prior to execution; its SHA-256 is archived (4a00a81629acfd3f1fb5d0a04cea795a52261270e7dc63bf7d3cb63cc11afda0). Confirmatory hypotheses: H1 — the guarded pipeline reduces first‑pass misconfiguration rate by ≥50% (relative) versus single‑shot generation; H2 — one or fewer automated repair iterations recover ≥75% of initially invalid configurations. The power plan used a planning baseline pass rate = 0.40 (explicit preregistered numeric assumption used in sample‑size planning). That planning assumption and the rest of the preregistration are archived and enumerated in the execution manifest referenced in the Disclosure Statement.

Design and sampling semantics: We used a paired within‑task design with 300 deterministically generated seeds from the frozen task generator. For each seed the same sampled LLM candidate (shared_initial_candidate semantics) was used for both arms: baseline (single‑shot generation) and guarded (the same candidate validated and—if invalid—subjected to up to one automated repair attempt). The shared‑candidate pairing was preregistered and reduces cross‑arm variability but also reduces the number of informative discordant pairs available to McNemar inference. Planned episodes = 600 (two episodes per seed); initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1; maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1.

Model, validator, and scoring: The declared model in the execution contract was gpt-5-mini. The frozen deterministic validator/repair adapter (validator id deterministic_netops_validator_v5) implements rule‑ and dependency‑based checks, canonicalizes configurations to normalized ASTs, and emits binary pass/fail scoring together with violation codes used for repair decisions. Scoring semantics applied full intent‑constraint validation: success requires the validator to observe required command sequences and dependency constraints. Model/provider failures were treated per the preregistered missingness plan (one retry allowed; primary analysis 'complete_pair_primary' drops pairs only if both calls fail).

Primary estimand and analysis plan: The primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. The preregistered primary test was the exact McNemar two‑sided test (α=0.05) on paired pass/fail outcomes. As preregistered we report the absolute paired difference and a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed fixed). Repair success is reported with exact Clopper–Pearson intervals. All analysis code and per‑task artifacts are archived in the execution manifest and the analysis artifact bundle referenced in the Disclosure Statement.
sections.results:
Execution accounting (archived): planned episodes = 600, completed episodes = 600, complete pairs = 300, model_calls_used = 301, repair‑stage invocations = 1. No provider or infrastructure failures occurred that affected planned sampling under the preregistered retry policy; full accounting is preserved in the execution manifest.

Primary outcomes (artifact‑derived): Baseline_success_count = 299/300 (99.6667%); Guarded_success_count = 300/300 (100.0%). Paired contingency: n11 = 299 (both success), n10 = 1 (guarded success, baseline fail), n01 = 0 (guarded fail, baseline success), n00 = 0 (both fail). These counts are produced directly from the archived contingency summary in the analysis artifact bundle and were used for confirmatory inference.

Statistical inference (preregistered computations applied to archived counts): Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00. Observed absolute paired difference (guarded minus baseline) = 1/300 ≈ 0.0033333. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI for the absolute paired difference = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). Repair outcomes (H2): the single allowed automated repair corrected the sole initially invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1); Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]. All numeric values are reported exactly as archived in the analysis outputs.

Post‑hoc sensitivity bound tied to archived contingency counts: with only one discordant pair (n10 + n01 = 1), the hard resolution limit on the absolute paired difference equals 1/300 ≈ 0.00333 (the observed point estimate). Under the observed paired semantics, the preregistered target effect (≈+0.30 absolute corresponding to a 50% relative reduction from the assumed baseline) is orders of magnitude larger than the resolvable improvement in this run; the observed near‑ceiling baseline therefore invalidates the preregistered power assumption and leaves negligible inferential power to detect the preregistered effect. The archived bootstrap CI upper bound (0.01) further bounds plausible absolute improvement under these sampling semantics. These sensitivity statements derive directly from the archived contingency counts and bootstrap outputs.

Representative diagnostic examples: Per‑task validator traces archived for every episode include normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation codes, and repair_applied flags. The single corrected baseline failure was remedied by invoking the preregistered repair adapter and revalidating; the final guarded configuration satisfied the intent constraints per the deterministic validator. Readers are referred to the archived execution manifest and analysis artifact bundle for full per‑task traces; those artifacts provide the granular evidence supporting the summarized counts above.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation and operational implications: The guarded pipeline corrected the only observed invalid baseline output, showing that a frozen deterministic validator plus a bounded automated repair iteration can remediate validator‑detected violations in at least some cases. However, this run does not provide confirmatory evidence for the preregistered large effect (≥50% relative reduction) because the empirical baseline pass rate was far higher than assumed in planning. The principal methodological lesson is that task‑bank calibration—ensuring a nontrivial baseline failure prevalence—is essential for informative paired inference when using shared‑candidate pairing semantics.

Design choices that affected inferential power: (1) Shared_initial_candidate pairing (preregistered) increased within‑pair correlation and reduced the expected number of informative discordant pairs for McNemar testing; this choice trades variance reduction against discordance information. (2) A single automated repair iteration bounds operational realism and reduces the potential for cumulative repair success; larger repair budgets or human verification loops would materially change the operational claim being tested. (3) The deterministic validator assesses canonicalized configuration constraints rather than executing runtime semantics; thus construct validity is limited with respect to packet‑level reachability or performance consequences.

Practical recommendations for future confirmatory NetOps experiments (artifact‑grounded): (a) Preregister and calibrate to expect a target number of initial failures (not only total N), and adjust task difficulty or adversarial augmentation to reach that failure prevalence; (b) explicitly preregister pairing semantics and compute their effect on expected discordant counts used in power calculations; (c) when operational claims require runtime assurances, incorporate emulation or simulation stages that exercise control‑plane and data‑plane consequences rather than relying solely on static validators; (d) report repair effectiveness as a conditional estimand (repair success conditional on initial failure) when baseline pass rates are uncertain.

Threats to validity (artifact‑tied): Internal validity: the shared‑candidate pairing and the single repair iteration were preregistered design choices that affect inference. Construct validity: the deterministic validator provides static configuration checks and canonicalization rather than live execution results. External validity: the synthetic task bank, constrained vendor‑template transformations, single model family (gpt-5-mini), and single validator implementation limit generality. Conclusion validity: the small number of discordant pairs (one) yields wide inferential uncertainty for large preregistered effects.
sections.conclusion: In this preregistered paired experiment (N=300 pairs) using a frozen deterministic validator and a one‑iteration automated repair budget applied to gpt‑5‑mini outputs, baseline single‑shot generation was near‑ceiling (299/300) and the guarded pipeline produced 300/300 valid outputs. The single automated repair corrected the only observed invalid baseline output, but the run does not support the preregistered claim of ≥50% relative reduction in misconfiguration because the observed baseline contradicted the planning assumption (planned baseline pass rate = 0.40) and left no statistical headroom. We recommend that future confirmatory NetOps evaluations (1) calibrate task banks to produce a prespecified number of initial failures, (2) explicitly preregister pairing semantics and repair budgets, and (3) when operational claims require runtime assurances, include emulation or simulation stages that exercise dynamic effects. All raw outputs, validator traces, repair traces, the execution manifest, and analysis artifacts are archived and enumerated in the execution manifest and analysis artifact bundle referenced in the Disclosure Statement.

limitations: Synthetic task bank and constrained vendor‑template scope limit external validity to broad production environments.
Single LLM (gpt-5-mini) and a single validator implementation restrict generality across model families and validator designs.
The preregistered power plan assumed a baseline pass rate = 0.40; the observed baseline (299/300) contradicts that assumption and removed headroom to detect the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction.
Sampling semantics (shared_initial_candidate) reused the same initial candidate across paired arms, increasing within‑pair correlation and reducing discordant pairs available to McNemar inference.

Validation used deterministic configuration/constraint checks rather than full dynamic emulation of runtime semantic effects; actual runtime consequences of configurations were not executed and remain unmeasured.

H2 repair‑success evidence is based on a single initially invalid case (1/1 → 100%), yielding a wide Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]; larger counts of initial failures are required to estimate repair effectiveness precisely.
